opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about quite a lot, partly because I'm in the slightly funny position of building these systems and also being a user of them every day.

The way I frame it for myself is that there are two kinds of leverage. The first is the obvious one: offloading the things that take time but not much thought. Summarizing a long thread, getting a first draft of something, writing a quick script to check an idea. That's useful, and honestly it adds up to a lot of hours, but it's not the most interesting part.

The second kind is where I think the real expansion happens: using the model as a thinking partner. When I'm exploring a research direction, I'll often just talk through it. "Here's the hypothesis, what am I missing? What's the strongest argument against this? Has something like this been tried?" It doesn't always give the right answer, but it widens the space of things I consider before I commit. In research, the expensive mistake isn't a bug in your code. It's spending three months going down the wrong path. Anything that helps you prune bad ideas earlier is enormously valuable.

There's also a learning side. I used to learn adjacent fields slowly: read the papers, ask colleagues, piece it together. Now I can get up to speed on, say, a corner of biology or a math technique much faster, because I can ask very specific questions at exactly my level of confusion. That's something a textbook can't do.

That said, I try to be careful about one thing. If you outsource too much of the thinking, you can lose the intuition that made you good in the first place. So I still like to do certain things the hard way, deriving something by hand or reading the original paper, because that's where taste comes from. The goal for me isn't to think less. It's to spend my thinking on the parts that matter most, and let the model handle more and more of the rest.

And of course, working on these models, every time I hit a limitation as a user, it goes straight onto the list of things we should fix. So it's a nice feedback loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, actually, because in some ways I'm in a slightly privileged position where I get to use these models before most people do, and I get to see where they're going. And honestly, my own usage has changed quite a bit over the last couple of years.

The way I'd frame it is: there are two very different modes. One is the mode where the model is a kind of very fast, very knowledgeable colleague that you can bounce ideas off. So if I'm thinking about a research direction, or I'm trying to understand some paper in an adjacent field that I don't have deep expertise in, I'll just have a conversation with Gemini about it. And the thing that's valuable there isn't that it gives me the answer, it's that it compresses the time it takes me to get to the point where I can ask the right question. That used to take me, you know, a day of reading. Now it's maybe an hour.

The second mode, which I think is the more interesting one and the one that's changing fastest, is delegation. Actually handing off a task and coming back later. And here I'll be honest, I was a bit skeptical for a while. Because as a researcher, a lot of what I do is not really that parallelizable, right? It's thinking. But what I've found is that there's a surprising amount of stuff around the thinking that is parallelizable. Writing the code to test a hypothesis, running an analysis on some logs, drafting a document. And once the models got good enough at that, you start to notice that your bottleneck shifts. The bottleneck is no longer "can I get this done," it's "do I know what I want done." Which is a much more interesting place to be as a bottleneck.

And I think that's the capacity expansion, really. It's not that I'm doing more of the same thing faster. It's that I can afford to try more things, because the cost of trying something went down a lot. In research, that matters enormously, because most ideas are wrong, and the faster you find out an idea is wrong, the more ideas you get to have.

There's also something I'd caution about, which is that it's quite easy to use these tools in a way that makes you feel more productive without actually being more productive. You generate a lot of text, you run a lot of experiments, and you lose the thread. So I've tried to be a bit disciplined about keeping the actual judgment with me. What's the question, is this result surprising, does this change what we should do next. I don't think I want to delegate that yet. Maybe eventually, but not yet.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as having a collaborator that helps me explore more ideas than I could on my own. A lot of research is moving between intuition and experimentation: you have an idea, you write some code, you look at the result, and you revise your thinking. AI can shorten that loop.

But expanding capacity also means helping me notice things I would otherwise miss. I can ask, “What’s the weakness in this argument? What experiment would distinguish these two explanations?” The value isn’t just getting an answer faster; it’s being able to ask a better question afterward.

You still need judgment. If you delegate your judgment along with the work, you can become very productive at going in the wrong direction. So I want assistance with exploring and testing ideas while staying engaged with what the evidence actually tells us.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as having a collaborator that helps me get from an intuition to something I can test. In research, you often have an idea that’s a little vague, and making it concrete takes a lot of work. You need to write some code, check an assumption, understand why an experiment failed. AI can help with all of those steps.

But the interesting question is what you do with that extra capacity. Do you just do the same things faster, or do you attempt something you wouldn’t have attempted before? For me, that second part is more exciting. If the cost of exploring an idea goes down, you can afford to be more curious.

You still need judgment. You need to decide which questions matter and whether the evidence actually supports your conclusion. Ideally, the AI gives you more room to exercise that judgment, while also challenging your thinking.
